questions.q: What's the first place to check when a SQL Agent job fails, according to this lesson?
options: sysjobhistory — the message column usually contains the real error verbatim, and most mistakes come from skipping straight to re-running the job instead
Immediately rewriting the job's T-SQL from scratch
The Windows Event Viewer, before checking anything in SQL Server
Deleting and recreating the job
questions.explain: Every job run writes history automatically — reading it first avoids re-diagnosing something SQL Server already told you.

questions.q: Why does knowing the specific step_id matter for a multi-step job?
options: It tells you exactly which step failed, and its subsystem/command, so you know precisely what to test manually outside of Agent
step_id has no practical use in troubleshooting
It only matters for jobs with a single step
It identifies which server the job ran on, not which part failed
questions.explain: A job failing overall tells you little; the specific step_id narrows it to exactly what needs testing.

questions.q: Why does a CmdExec or PowerShell step commonly fail even when its logic is completely correct?
options: It runs as the SQL Server Agent service account by default, not the DBA's own login — if that account lacks a specific permission, the step fails regardless of correct logic
CmdExec and PowerShell steps never actually run under any security context
These step types always run with full administrator rights
This only happens if the job has more than one step
questions.explain: This is the specific, frequently misdiagnosed cause this lesson highlights — DBAs often assume the code is wrong when it's actually a permissions gap.

questions.q: What is the more secure, more correct fix for a step failing due to service-account permissions, per this lesson?
options: Configuring a dedicated proxy account scoped to only what that specific step needs, rather than widening the Agent service account's own permissions
Granting the Agent service account full sysadmin rights
Disabling security entirely for that job
Running every job step as the job owner regardless of subsystem
questions.explain: Widening the shared service account's permissions is the less secure option — a scoped proxy account is the better fix.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the "other frequent causes" of job failure named in this lesson, beyond the service account?
options: Context differences — a T-SQL step that works fine manually in SSMS can fail under the job owner's different default database or permission set
SQL Server Agent jobs can only ever fail due to permissions issues
Jobs never fail due to scheduling conflicts
Dependent resources are never a real cause of job failures
questions.explain: Schedule conflicts, a not-yet-ready dependent resource, and context differences are all named as real, frequent causes distinct from the service-account issue.
